newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal rejects idea it weakens single currency.
newsitem.headline: Portugal rejects idea it weakens single currency.

text.p: Prime Minister Antonio Guterres firmly rejected on Thursday suggestions that the inclusion of Portugal amongst European Union countries to launch the planned single currency would weaken it.

As parliament prepared on Thursday to debate a rare joint motion tabled by the government and its main opposition backing Portugal's entry to economic and monetary union (EMU) in the first wave, Guterres said that the Portuguese escudo posed no threat to the future European currency, the euro.
"The escudo, integrated into the euro, in no way will weaken it," he said in an interview with O Publico newspaper.

The Socialist leader said that Portugal had given ample proof of its financial and economic health and that an economy accounting for less than one percent of total European Union activity was in any case too small to be an unsettling factor in EMU at its launch in January 1999.

"Even those who are worried about the strength of the euro...must recognise that the entry of Portugal into the initial 'hard core' of monetary union in no way casts doubt on its solidity," Guterres said.

In recent weeks doubts have emerged in some northern European countries about the wisdom of letting their southern European partners Spain, Italy and Portugal -- the so-called 'Club Med' -- into EMU from the start.

German bankers, fearing the euro could turn out weaker than the mark, have been particularly vocal in expressing concerns that Europe's southern flank, with its history of financial instability, might not be ready for the discipline of monetary union even if the countries passed nominal entry tests.

But Portugal, which is arguably the best-placed economically of the three southern candidates, has been adamant that if it meets the stiff entry tests, which will be set on economic performance in 1997, then nobody can keep it out.

The message was underlined in the unprecedented joint motion of support for Portugal's EMU bid being put to parliament on Thursday by the government and its centre-right opposition, the Social Democrats.
Although the Social Democrats are firmly pro-European, the debate marks the first time that they have been prepared to align openly with the government in a parliamentary vote.
Parliamentary support for the motion reaffirming Portugal's commitment to EMU is guaranteed as the two parties together hold some 85 percent of the seats in the 230-seat National Assembly.

The motion also "expresses concern and disagreement with public declarations of political leaders from other European Union countries that put in doubt the spirit and letter" of Europe's Maastricht Treaty, the blueprint for monetary union.

Maastricht lays down the terms and conditions for entry to the single currency which include a three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) ceiling for the public sector deficit and limits on inflation.
Most economic analysts believe that Portugal has a good chance of meeting the terms.

Guterres, who will speak in the Thursday debate, said in the interview that doubts being voiced in Germany probably had more to do with local uncertainties about that country's own economic performance.
"I think that there is a crisis of confidence in Germany...and this makes some observers adopt an excessively fearful stance on the euro," he said.
